documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence has moved from a research promise to a clinical reality, functioning less as a replacement for practitioners than as a force multiplier that extends the reach, speed, and consistency of expert judgment across the care continuum. This review synthesizes the state of the field as of 2025, organizing the evidence around three connected questions: what artificial intelligence now does well in clinical decision making and operations, where its risks concentrate, and why implementation remains the binding constraint on realized value. It traces the conceptual evolution of the field from rule-based expert systems through statistical machine learning and deep learning to the foundation models and large language models that now dominate attention. Diagnostic and predictive applications have matured fastest, with imaging triage, early-warning models for deterioration and sepsis, and medication safety tools demonstrating strong discriminative performance and, in a growing number of cases, prospective and randomized evidence. Efficiency applications, most visibly ambient documentation systems, have produced some of the most consistent real-world gains, reducing documentation time and clinician burnout at scale. Against these advances sit persistent risks: algorithmic bias that can widen rather than narrow disparities, brittleness under distribution shift, automation bias and alert fatigue at the human interface, opacity that complicates accountability, unresolved questions of medicolegal liability, and privacy and cybersecurity exposure. Reporting and evaluation standards specific to artificial intelligence have emerged to raise the evidentiary bar, and the regulatory environment has responded with lifecycle-oriented frameworks, predetermined change control plans, and transparency expectations, yet a durable gap remains between marketing authorization and demonstrated clinical benefit. The central argument is that the value of clinical artificial intelligence is determined less by model accuracy in isolation than by the quality of the sociotechnical system into which a model is placed: governance, workflow integration, monitoring, and the preservation of meaningful human oversight. The review closes with a practical agenda for closing the gap between capability and dependable, equitable benefit.

documents.abstract: This research presents a systematic literature review of Agentic Artificial Intelligence (Agentic AI) in the construction industry. The study aims to consolidate the emerging and fragmented body of knowledge on Agentic AI and examine how autonomous, goal-directed, reasoning, planning, memory, tool-use, and adaptive capabilities are being developed and applied across construction projects and the wider Architecture, Engineering and Construction sector. The review follows the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) methodology. Peer-reviewed journal articles were identified through systematic searches of Scopus and Web of Science and screened using predefined eligibility criteria concerning publication characteristics, construction relevance, intelligent or adaptive behaviour, and autonomous decision-making. The final review comprises 50 journal articles published between 2021 and 2026. The study examines five main areas. It investigates the conceptual evolution and defining characteristics of Agentic AI in construction, architectural paradigms and intelligence mechanisms, enabling technologies, applications and reported outcomes across the construction lifecycle, and the technical, organisational, governance, and ethical barriers affecting implementation. The review also examines the methodological and validation approaches used in existing studies to assess the maturity of current evidence. The expected outcomes include a structured synthesis of the current state of Agentic AI in construction, identification of major research and implementation gaps, and development of a future research agenda. Building on the systematic evidence, the study also proposes the Human-Governed Construction Agentic Intelligence Loop (H-CAIL), a construction-specific closed-loop conceptual framework integrating project context and data, multimodal perception, goal-directed planning, reasoning, memory, tool selection, human-governed action, evaluation, and adaptive learning. The framework is intended to provide a conceptual basis for developing trustworthy and human-governed Agentic AI systems capable of supporting construction decision-making and project delivery across the asset lifecycle.

documents.abstract: Learning theories have historically changed when the conditions of learning evolved. Generative and agentic AI create a new condition by allowing learners to delegate explanation, writing, problem solving, and other cognitive work to systems that can generate, recommend, and sometimes act on the learner’s behalf. This creates a fundamental challenge for learning theory: successful performance can no longer be assumed to indicate learning. Learners may complete tasks effectively with AI support while developing less understanding, weaker judgment, and limited transferable capability. We argue that this problem is not fully captured by existing learning theories. Behaviourism, cognitivism, constructivism, and connectivism remain important, but they do not directly explain when AI-assisted performance becomes durable human capability. We propose Agentivism, a learning theory for human-AI interaction. Agentivism defines learning as durable growth in human capability through selective delegation to AI, epistemic monitoring and verification of AI contributions, reconstructive internalization of AI-assisted outputs, and transfer under reduced support. The importance of Agentivism lies in explaining how learning remains possible when intelligent delegation is easy and human-AI interaction is becoming a persistent and expanding part of human learning. The theory yields six testable propositions and suggests that teachers preserve opportunities for learner judgement while researchers distinguish AI-assisted performance from capability that endures beyond immediate support.

documents.abstract: Advanced AI systems can generate substantial benefits in science, engineering, medicine, productivity, and public services while also creating misuse, malfunction, systemic, and loss-of-control risks. This paper proposes the AI Authority Control Framework (AACF), a sociotechnical framework for bounding consequential authority rather than treating model capability alone as the central safety variable. AACF distinguishes Granted, Obtainable, Deferred, and Systemic Authority; separates technical execution authority (AAL) from systemic influence (SIL); and specifies external control-plane, credential-mediation, authority-budget, safe-transition, human-oversight, governance, and portfolio controls. It introduces hard deployment gates for self-escalation, self-governance, uncontained persistence or replication, unilateral catastrophic authority, and other configurations that could make meaningful human control practically unrecoverable. The framework is complementary to alignment: alignment seeks to reduce the probability that dangerous behavior is attempted, while authority control seeks to limit the consequences of error, misuse, deception, or emergent behavior. To challenge the framework, the paper reports two rounds of adversarial theoretical review and retrospective validation against documented failures in software, cybersecurity, aviation, critical infrastructure, and agentic AI. It also defines a staged validation program culminating in controlled sandbox experiments that compare prompt-only safeguards with externally enforced controls. The central proposition is that advanced AI can become more useful without automatically receiving greater authority when access, permissions, resources, delegation, and consequential actions remain independently bounded and auditable across the surrounding sociotechnical system.

documents.abstract: Scientific fieldwork is an essential component of research across many academic disciplines. Fieldwork entails numerous risks, ranging from interpersonal to environmental risks, and can often result in physical and mental injury or illness. Despite these potential harms, standardized frameworks for understanding, managing, and responding to incidents in fieldwork remain underdeveloped. A limited understanding of incident causation in fieldwork contexts compounds this gap. In this article we propose that fieldwork, like other workplaces, operates as a complex socio-technical system in which people, cultural beliefs, governance, equipment, and the environment interact to create both safe and unsafe outcomes. To better understand the scientific fieldwork system, we conducted four focus groups to identify the people and institutions that constitute a fieldwork system and to characterize how these actors are organized within hierarchical levels. Through these sessions, we developed a classificatory scheme of variables that together influence safety outcomes. In total, 91 different actors across seven hierarchical levels and a contextual domain were identified. The resulting ActorMap and associated contributory factors offer a foundational framework for operationalizing safety and risk approaches, such as AcciMapping, in fieldwork settings. By incorporating these insights, we can enhance training, policy development, and institutional support structures to better equip researchers for the challenges of fieldwork

Work fatigue is a common occupational health and safety (OHS) issue among healthcare workers. It may reduce work productivity and service quality while increasing the likelihood of work-related errors. High service demands, limited healthcare personnel, and excessive workloads may further contribute to the occurrence of fatigue. This study aimed to identify factors associated with work fatigue among healthcare workers at Public Health Centers in Pondok Aren District. A quantitative analytical study with a cross-sectional design was conducted involving 187 healthcare workers selected through total sampling. The independent variables included age, sex, educational level, length of employment, workload, and exercise habits, while work fatigue served as the dependent variable. Data were analyzed using univariate analysis, bivariate analysis with the chi-square test, and multivariate analysis through logistic regression. The findings indicated that 114 respondents (61%) experienced moderate work fatigue, while 73 respondents (39%) experienced high work fatigue. Significant associations were found between fatigue and length of employment, workload, and exercise habits. Multivariate analysis identified workload as the most dominant factor associated with work fatigue. The Nagelkerke R Square value of 0.324 indicated that the model explained 32.4% of the variation in work fatigue.

Patient experiences reported online can reveal safety incidents in healthcare organisations, but they can only translate into quality improvement if organisations engage with them. Accordingly, healthcare organisations’ responses to online feedback offer a new data source on corrective culture, namely, the norms and practices for identifying, interpreting, and acting on safety incidents. This study explored the feasibility of using a large language model to reliably code these responses for two candidate indicators of corrective culture: engagement and organisational learning. We manually coded 600 feedback-response pairs for engagement (κ = 0.90) and organisational learning (Gwet’s AC1 = 0.84), and used this gold standard to develop and evaluate a GPT-5-mini classifier. The classifier coded engagement with high agreement (F1 = 0.86), but was less reliable for organisational learning (F1 = 0.70). To assess construct validity, we analysed human disagreements and classifier misclassifications. Organisational learning was harder to code because it is a reported behaviour, whereas engagement is an observed behaviour. We then used the classifier to code 157,051 responses (2011–2023) across 844 healthcare organisations. Our results indicate that large language models can reliably code engagement in these responses, while their ability to code organisational learning remains inconclusive. Organisational culture in healthcare is usually assessed with staff surveys, which rely on self-report. Large language models could complement surveys by measuring observed behaviour in naturally occurring data, although whether engagement reflects corrective culture requires external validation.

Artificial intelligence has recently become an important part of high school learning, which facilitates the learning process by providing students with viable alternative learning sources, feedback, and news. Today, the issue of the impact of artificial intelligence-based learning units, along with rapidly evolving learning-unit systems and content, on adolescent cognitive skills is emerging. This paper reviews literature on artificial intelligence-based high school learning, discussing the effects of these learning units on cognitive off-loading, motivation to learn, and self-regulated learning in order to bring out both the advantages and disadvantages associated with high school education. It maintains that artificial intelligence contains advantages of optimising learning and coming out with useful information when utilised as an assistant to a human being, however, the danger of human-critical thought development, built-in intrinsic motivation, and depending on the AI to provide solutions to social issues is there because of extreme reliance on artificial intelligence. In a nutshell, this review implores the stakeholders- high schools and students- to provide the requisite guidelines for AI exploration, and critical thinking development.

The relationship between creativity and artificial intelligence (AI) has attracted widespread attention from the public, corporations, and academia. Advanced AI-based examples of artistic production, such as AI generated music, poetry, and paintings, have started transforming the creative and cultural industries. This study analyzed the componential model of creativity through the lens of the Generative AI (GenAI) artwork produced by artists. A qualitative approach was employed utilizing data collected from interviews with various artists, critics, and technicians who worked with GenAI, thereby helping in identifying the creativity paradoxes in the AI era. The results suggest that the use of GenAI has created dualities in the components of creativity, including tensions between extrinsic and intrinsic motivations, artistic and technical skills, and creations by an artist and those generated by AI. Given that AI will continue to develop, the cultural and creative industries need to find ways to navigate these creativity paradoxes.
